title: 'Ritual, "Just" Do It, Ji and Ri'
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of approaching spiritual practice with a mindset of ritualized awareness, letting go of expectations and attachments. By doing so, we can connect with ourselves and others more deeply and find balance between distinctions and appreciation for impermanence. This approach encourages us to look within and trust our own intuition, rather than relying on external authorities or intellectual understanding, allowing us to access wisdom in everyday moments and relationships.

sentences.text: Welcome, everybody.
Well, we're co-creating a pretty interesting day, aren't we?
Interesting, wonderful, challenging, surprising, annoying, energizing, exhausting.
Just another day, really, right?
Just like any other day.
Except we're doing it in what seems like a particular way.
I was thinking today about what seems extra interesting to me about our sesshin practice: the way the whole thing is like one big ritual.
I think at first it might appear like it's a meditation retreat with some ritual sort of glue, so that we can manage to sit that much.
I don't think it really is that way.
I think actually the whole thing is one giant ritual, one big complex ritual, every moment of everything we do.
The way we move and sit and stand and walk is all ritual, ritualized.
The talking we do is ritual, too.
Even as we try to keep the silence, when we open our mouths it's chanting.
It's the usual announcements.
Even this, this is the same stuff I say every time.
It's all a ritual.
The eating is so ritualized.
Thank you everybody for pulling off the eating and the cooking that made the eating, and the serving.
So we can see that eating is a ritual.
So everything is a ritual.
And in fact even the zazen, which seems like some kind of meditation at first, like something we'll do in order to calm down or see things more clearly, the zazen is a ritual, too.
Tomorrow, if you can come tomorrow morning, Chris is going to give a talk on Dogen's great essay on zazen, Fukanzazengi.
And we've all chanted that many times.
Probably you noticed he says in there, zazen is not meditation.
It says right in there.
The word meditation, like a lot of words, gives us the idea that something's going to result or something's going to happen.
Maybe it will, maybe it won't.
Of course he's turning that around, helping us to see that we do things just to do them, not to get something, which is what ritual is, right?
You do it just to do it.
So sitting zazen, just to sit zazen.
And so I think the word in there looks like an ordinary little connector word in English: just.
Sit, just to sit.
Do zazen, just to do zazen.
Walk, just walk.
Wash the dishes, just wash the dishes.
It's funny, we do expect probably the dishes to be clean again, but they're going to be dirty, right?
So why do we think that there's some kind of human potential, meditation something, that will clean us up so we won't get dirty again?
Doesn't make sense.
So we sit just to sit as messy human beings, dirty and clean, clean and dirty.
So it seems like we're doing a ritual today, is all we're really doing.
We're not doing a meditation intensive exactly, but maybe we're doing a "just" intensive.
Re-learning how to just do things.
Just do one thing after the next, which isn't that complicated, but somehow we lose track of that basic ability to just do one thing.
Just do one thing wholeheartedly and with full presence.
Which can be an adjustment, we have to shift gears if we're not doing it that way usually, but what a relief too.
What a relief, I only have to just do one thing.
I was thinking this morning when I woke up so early that a lot of things feel complicated or challenging in life, for me anyway, but this doesn't feel that way anymore.
It's like [unclear: "just so, let's be fine"], we just do.
And then the mind can go, oh, but it's so complicated, [unclear: "what is such and so it doesn't bring to this, or the"].
And the mind can throw up all kinds of anxiety.
Different Tenzos, for instance, have different plans.
Tenzo Bob Rose is always bustling around at 5 a.m. and making coffee and being cheerful and down there.
He's reasonably quiet but he's putting out some energy.
And I got in there at 5:30 and there was no Tenzo.
So Tenzo Ben had a different plan.
So my mind could definitely go, uh oh, what if something happened?
What if there's no food?
What if Ben forgot, or something, I don't know.
Any thought I have is not charitable at that point, because of course Ben had it all figured out and organized and didn't need to be there at 5:30 bustling around.
So the mind can make it complicated, but actually yeah, it's pretty simple.
We just show up and do what we do.
We have this complicated ritual to help us see that,
and it's also a complicated ritual which involves intense trust, and interconnection and interrelationship with each other.
Everyone trusting each other as best we can.
And then we have those little moments when we don't quite trust each other.
We bump into each other and we learn from that.
So it's just being and just doing and just getting confused and just remembering.
So I forgot my oryoki set.
It's right by the door, too.
So I had a flash of just being annoyed with myself, and I closed the back door and said, where's my oryoki set?
Oh, it's at home.
I don't have time to go get it.
But it always works out.
In this case, there's been an abandoned oryoki set on the windowsill for about a calendar year.
It's like, oh, I'll use that one and then I can clean it and put it away.
So it works out.
So relearning this ability to just be, to just be okay.
To just do one thing is to just be okay.
And then it's not really even about the stuff that we're doing, the activities.
It's about these beings, these luminous beings in the middle of activity, shining their light on each other, receiving each other's light.
Dogen says, "Turn the light inwardly and illuminate the self."
I think really what he means, maybe it's not the best English translation, what he means is: notice that the inward light already was illuminating the self.
And it always was.
We're just so good at getting in our own way, blocking our own light.
So this ritual seems to be a ritual in which we remember and we see that.

We see our light shining through, and we feel and remember that even when we're annoyed that we forgot something or doubting somebody or whatever, even in the middle of confusion or those little moments of suffering, and those are moments of suffering, in the middle of everything, this luminous being, Buddha, luminous being, awakened being.
But we forget this thoroughly enough that it sounds ridiculous when someone says to us, you're a Buddha.
So we don't usually go around saying that, because it just confuses people, but it's true.
It probably should.
Edie and Seishin in different ways suggested a little practice, that this practice period maybe some of us will just change our label for a while and we can be known by our Dharma name.
So you can call me Nomon if you want, instead of Tim.
It's just a label.
But we might as well call each other Buddha.
Hi Buddha, how are you?
I'm good, Buddha.
How could I not be good?
I'm Buddha.
Why do you even need to ask?
So this ritual today seems like it's about all this stuff,
oryoki, all these Japanese words, doans and kyokyos and inos and tantos and all this.
But maybe it's actually just a reminder that every day really can be this way.
Every day could be a ritual.
Every day could be just doing one thing.
Every day could be opening up and showing up as our luminous selves.
It's pretty great.
And we have to forgive ourselves in advance that we're going to forget again.
I'll forget again.
Maybe you won't.
Maybe you will.
But luckily we have another sesshin on the calendar, and then we'll show up and we can have the same talk again and go, all right.
So there's nothing new.
There's nothing new here.
It's old.
And our culture denigrates the old, right?
Same old, same old, boring.
It's the beautiful old.
That's our wise old selves, our old souls.
And of course the conditioned world still exists.
We still need all this stuff.
We need the things of the world.
In our class on the poem Sandokai, the merging of difference and unity,
which luckily we chanted this morning, that was handy, we're unpacking this idea that things matter.
We need things.
But things are so sticky and lead to suffering if we relate to them in a certain way.
We're unpacking the line in there.
It's the seventh line of the poem.
*Grasping at things is surely delusion.*
*Grasping at things is surely delusion.* The busy things of the world are here.
And even when we practice sesshin and turn off our phones and try to forget about all the things that bother us out there in the bigger world, we still bring it.
We bring all the things of the world within us.
So there's this character in the text,
Chinese character that the Japanese call G, things.
Trying to keep these, learn this.
All the commentators on this text make a big deal of these two characters.
G, which means things.
And then the next line says,
*Merging with sameness is still not enlightenment.*
So sameness there is a rendering of G's friend, Ri.
Ri points to the way everything is just as it is.
Someone was telling me, isn't it great the way in sesshin you remember that everything's okay?
That's the Ri.
But the Sandokai says, well, it's not a matter of just sort of kicking G out of the equation.
We need G.
It's not a matter of just merging with Ri, with sameness, with enlightenment, with awakening, with luminousness, with non-thingness.
It's really about letting them play together, letting them intertwine in just the way that they do, without getting in the way so much.
So thus, just walking, just chopping, just eating is G and Ri,
is things and non-things, is suffering and awakening, is relative and absolute.
And the things are a vehicle.
The things are essential.
To enact this deep sesshin life, we need a lot of gear, a lot of things, physical things in the room,
and mental things.
And it's good to remember that in this way of thinking, there's no real difference between the physical things and the mental things.
It's a false distinction.
We show up full of mental things, all of us.
Our thoughts, our opinions, our memories, our ideas of how it's supposed to go or not.
And even our identity, a bunch of mental things.
So we need these mental things.
We need this realm of things, the realm of G.
And maybe what this ritual day of sesshin helps us do is remember that we can handle and hold things, mental things and physical things, with a certain spirit, the spirit of Ri,
the spirit of beyond things, the spirit of openness, the spirit of luminosity, the spirit of Buddha.

One time, Norman, years and years ago, he probably forgets this now, said he got into Zen because he had this feeling like he was really clumsy and he needed to learn how to hold things, how to use his hands.
It struck me, like, how to use your hands?
I'm here to get peace, man.
Who cares about my hands?
And it is interesting the way ritual spaces have a feeling to them, isn't it?
This is the interplay between the inner and the outer things of a ritual life.
When you come in here, there's a feeling to it.
People feel it, even if they don't know any of this terminology or whatever.
There's a feeling to everything placed just so.
Someone was telling me that the other day.
I came to visit a non-Buddhist meditation group that meets here, actually.
I visit them once a month or so.
And in the non-Buddhist meditation,
sometimes I do guidance and I talk during the meditation.
So I didn't do that, I just rang the bell and we just sat for half an hour.
I was saying, well, how was that?
I didn't give you any suggestions.
And one of the people said, when I come in here and I sit with you,
I just, something happens, I feel something.
It was interesting.

I was thinking, even if we studied about Soto Zen Buddhism and how it's done and read lots of books, and then we went out and bought all the right stuff and we arranged it just like it does in the book, it would be like creating a museum.
But I bet it wouldn't have the same feeling.
Somehow we need to practice with all this stuff and practice with each other, our mental things and physical things, the harmony and the disharmony and the harmony returning.
That's what seems to generate this feeling.
So we do need to learn stuff.
It's good to study, know a little about the history, the sutras, the texts.

I was actually suffering a little bit on Wednesday trying to say something that made any sense about this weird Chinese poem that we chant, and I went, well, I have to try to say something, we chant this poem all the time.
I was trying to push it into the realm of understandable things and it wasn't budging.
So finally, hopefully, we'll all just relax and appreciate it for what it is.
Forty-two lines, five characters each, of Chinese poetry with an English translation talking about things and beyond things.
There's not a lot of practical psychological advice in there.
It's about the essence of everything.
And that poem and a lot of the stories of Buddhism use the metaphor of light and dark, lightness and darkness.
And I think light and dark are used a little differently than we usually use them in the West.
There's overlap.
But often in the West, light means good, right?
Light is positive and dark means bad or evil.
What a dark character.
But in Buddhism, and maybe more broadly in Asia, I'm not really sure, it's a little bit different.
Light means this sense of things.
Light means distinguishing things.
Mental things, physical things, nameable things can be seen in the light, right?
The light of consciousness shines on them and we can see.
There's a cup and a lectern and a complex being I call Kate.
Maybe I should call her Ryushin instead.
And darkness means in the absence of light, you can't see the boundaries and edges of things anymore.
It's not so easy to name them and distinguish them in the dark.
And we don't have to be threatened or afraid of that.
We can appreciate the deep healing value of turning off the lights.
Not doing that all the time, but not distinguishing and categorizing things and then having preferences about them and opinions and theories and philosophies.
We need all that, but we need to be able to turn it off again, too.
Or maybe to appreciate that it exists and it doesn't.
That's why the Sandokai goes on about how in the light there is darkness, but don't take it as darkness.
In the dark there is light, don't see it as light.
We need dark and we need light.
That's one seamless reality.
So we learn more stuff at [unclear: "Cast Light"], that's wonderful.
We try to make sense of things in our lives, in this tradition and whatever we're trying to do.
It's also wonderful that these teachings and this practice encourage us not to do that.
To do it and to not do it.
Or to do it with the spirit of not doing it.
Turn on the light and look around and recognize you can't see everything.
It's a little bit like going out into the wilderness.
Such a wonderful thing to do.
Out beyond the city lights, standing in a meadow on a moonless night, you can only see so far, right?
You know there's a lot more that you can't see.
So maybe in sesshin today we can really appreciate what we can see with our consciousness, with light.
We can really appreciate what we can't see: the darkness outside that circle, or mixed into that circle, or something.
The next story in the Mumonkan collection is also about this.
Handily.
We're up to case 28 out of 48.
It's probably going to take me another year.
Sorry, you're going to have to keep hearing about this stuff to get through this book.
But in the light I made a vow, so I have to keep going.
There are two figures in this story, a teacher and a student having interactions, which is common.
The teacher is named Longtan, and the Japanese say Ryutan.
And the student is named Deshan.
Deshan.
Japanese say Tokusan.
So that's another level of confusion: multiple names for everybody.
It may be some light, but the light's bouncing all around in these Zen stories.
It's like a hall of mirrors with light.
The title of every case is four characters.
From the Sandokai you may have a sense of what's behind these English translations that are all so different, because things are hard to translate from Chinese.
And there are rules.
It's always supposed to be this many characters.
So the Chinese composers had to cram in and pick four characters.
Maybe the idea they had for this required five or six.
Too bad for them.
Four is what you get.
The four characters that are the title of this story literally mean Lungtong Long Ring.
Lungtong the name.
Long like a long time.
Ring like ringing a bell.
Lungtong Long Ring.
Robert Aitken translated that as Lungtong renowned far and wide.
The word "renowned" is not in there at all, but he assumed that's what is meant: something is heard far and wide.
Other translators just look at what the story is about, ignore the Chinese, and call this story Lungtong Blows Out a Candle, which is where he's going, as you'll see.
So that's interesting.
Sometimes the translators don't want to bother us with the original because it's confusing, and they just make something else up.
That's not what it says.
For me that's what we're always doing when we try to shine light on things that are dark and we're talking about it: we're just giving our idea.
Here's what I see.
And we don't say "here's what I see," do we?
We say, "this is what is.
This is true."
So anyway, here's the story.
Some of these stories are pretty minimalistic, as you've seen, and this one is a long story, and the commentary has a long back story.
So this is like storytelling around the fire.
Here's the story.
*Deishan, the student, visited Lungtong and questioned him sincerely far into the night.
It grew late and Lungtong said, "Why don't you retire?"
Deishan made his bows and lifted the blinds to withdraw, but was met by darkness.
It's late.
And turning back he said, "It's dark outside."
So Lungtong lit a candle and handed it to Deishan.
Deishan was about to take it, and he walked back to his room, when Lungtong blew it out.
At this Deishan had a sudden realization and made bows.
Lungtong said, "What truth did you discern?"
Deishan said, "From now on I will not doubt the words of an old priest who is renowned everywhere under the sun."*
I'm going to see where Aitken got "renowned" in that line.
*From now on I will not doubt the words of an old priest who is renowned everywhere under the sun.
The next day, Lungtong took the high seat before his assembly to give a talk, and said, "I see a brave fellow among you monks.
His fangs are like a sword tree, his mouth is like a blood bowl.
Give him a blow and he won't even turn his head.
Someday we will climb the highest peak and establish our way there."
Then Deishan brought out his notes on the Diamond Sutra.
He brought them out before the Dharma Hall,*
so this must have been after the talk, so out in the courtyard in front of the Dharma Hall,
*he brought out his Diamond Sutra notes and held up a torch saying, "Even though you have exhausted the abstruse doctrines, that is like placing a hair in a vast space.
Even though you have learned all the secrets of the world, it is like letting a single drop of water fall into an enormous valley."
And then he burned up all his notes, making his bow as he took his leave.*
It says he took his leave with his teachers, and maybe after the talk they all filed out and Deishan sprung up and did this trick.
It's not the usual thing to do, probably.
It would be kind of like if I went out to the lobby first and you came in and I was ready to burn up my notes.
So that's the story.
The story itself is three parts.
First, the teacher and student have a private conversation late into the night, the student trying to understand all this stuff, trying to understand the things of practice.
Finally the teacher says, you better just go to bed.
He's about to step out into the dark, but it's dark out there.
The teacher gives him a candle.
The teacher blows out the candle.
It's a great moment of clarity, of seeing in the dark, right?
Literally it's an example of seeing in the dark.
And the teacher recognizes that something happened, and he says, well, I won't doubt you anymore.
I won't doubt the teachers anymore.
Then the teacher praises him in front of the whole assembly, which is kind of wild.
It would be kind of intense if I did that, right?
"Oh, gathered members of Red Cedar, I'm very happy to say that I see someone among you who will one day climb the seat."
Like, who is he talking about?
And then they leave the talk and the student gets out all these notes and burns them up in this great little speech.
Okay, so that's the story, that's the case.
Here's the back story in Wu Man's comment.
*Before Deishan crossed the border from his native province, his mind was burning and his mouth was sputtering.
Full of arrogance, he went south to exterminate the doctrine of a special transmission outside of the sutras.
When he reached the road to Liqou, he sought to buy refreshments from an old woman.
He found a tea stand.
The old woman looked at him and said, "Your reverence, what sort of literature do you have in your cart?"*
He must have had so many commentaries and notes that he needed an entire cart.
Other times I heard this story told he had a backpack, but this says he had a cart.
She looks and sees he has boxes and boxes of books or something.
*The old woman selling tea says, "Your reverence, what sort of literature do you have there in your cart?"
Deishan said, "Notes and commentaries in the Diamond Sutra."
The old woman said, "I hear the Diamond Sutra says, past mind cannot be grasped, present mind cannot be grasped, future mind cannot be grasped.
Which mind does your reverence intend to refresh?"
Deishan was dumbfounded, unable to answer.
He did not expire completely under her words.
However, he asked, "Is there a teacher of Zen Buddhism in the neighborhood?"*
That's what it says.
*The old woman said, "Ah, the priest Lungtan is about a half a mile from here, up the road."*
It doesn't say whether he still had his tea or not.
And then it says:
*Arriving at Lungtan's place, Deishan was utterly defeated.
His earlier words certainly did not match his later ones.
But Lungtan*
(this is Muman who collected the story)
*but Lungtan disgraced himself in his compassion for his son.
Finding a bit of live coal in the [unclear: "other"], he took up muddy water and drenched him, destroying everything at once.
Viewing the matter dispassionately, you can see it was all a farce.*
So the old commentary thought Lungtan could have been better in training Deishan.
The backstory behind this story is that Deishan was a well-known, popular Buddhist teacher in the north part of China.
It's unclear how literally true this was, but China is divided into northern and southern kingdoms in this era.
This is like the seventh, eighth century, something like that.
The Buddhism that was predominant in the north was supposedly very scholarly and step-by-step, and you knew what to do next.
The crowd had a curriculum.
Buddhism in the north had a curriculum.
And the Buddhism of the south, in this trope, was more spontaneous and intuitive and, you know, Zen.
So Deishan was an established teacher, had Dharma transmission, all this stuff.
He really loved the Diamond Sutra, which is a great text.
And it's a text about emptiness.
It's not a text about step-by-step.
It's a text about understanding that nothing can be understood.
And he was probably a pretty good teacher.
It was the other idea.
It wasn't just [unclear: "adult"].
They heard that in the south they weren't even studying the Diamond Sutra.
They weren't doing these step-by-step scholarly studies like they should.
So he packed up all his stuff and figured he'd go straight into the mountain.
And his first deep experience was that there's something more to this than step-by-step, something in the darkness beyond the words, right?
So he's a teacher in the light.
The first teacher was this woman at the tea stand.
Sadly, her name is not recorded, nor any details about her life.
One assumes she was probably also a student of Luangtaan.
And she certainly had a deep understanding that helped [unclear: "Yiger"] Deshan.
These stories are about a pretty patriarchal culture and system of practice, and there's a bunch of stories about men, so we'll need to for sure study the woman teachers.
But it's wonderful to honor and celebrate when a few women manage to slip through the male hegemony recorded in the old stories.
Deep bows to the tea seller, whatever her name was.
And then there's another story in between these two stories.
So first he crosses the border with all his stuff and is bested by the tea lady, and heads up to the local monastery to see what else he can learn.
But on the half mile or whatever up to the monastery, he must have gathered up his pride again, I guess.
Pride is like those toys that wobble and don't fall down.
And he was thinking about the name of the teacher, which is also the name of the monastery and the mountain, Luangtaan, which is pronounced Ryutan in Japanese, Sino-Japanese voicing.
So Ryu is the same Ryu in [unclear: "Kate here's"] name, it's the dragon.
And Tan, pronounced more or less the same in both, is a pond.
So he's thinking, oh okay, I'm going to go visit the dragon in the pond.
Wow, okay.
So when Deshan had his first interview with Luangtaan, he says, according to this, *I've heard of the renowned Luangtaan, but I see no dragon or pond.* So he's got all prideful again.
And Luangtaan replies, *You yourself have arrived at Luangtaan.

You yourself have entered the dragon's pond.* There are a lot of stories like this where the student comes up a little prideful and says, I don't see such a great teaching here, and the teacher just keeps his or her composure and just offers Dharma.
You have arrived at the dragon pond.
You have arrived.
You yourself are here.
In other words, keep studying, keep studying, young Padawan.
You will realize your dragon nature.
You already have it.
You already are a luminous Buddha.
You're suffering right now.
You're hung up on things.
You're only in the light, but you'll feel the darkness.
And you are in the darkness.
Too bad you don't get it yet, but you will.
And then the main story happens.
He really wants to understand this, and he keeps studying with his teacher and even convinces his teacher to have long one-on-one conversations in what might be a big monastery, we don't know.
And finally he turns to leave and says, it's dark out there.
The teacher gives him a light and blows it out.
That's what it would be if we let our light blow out and felt the darkness a little more in this ritual day of sesshin, like these two old worthies.
And if we think we are something special, the only thing we have to do is go to Starbucks or the woods or one of our independent coffee shops and the Wise Barista, [unclear: "Letters Treats Coffee"].
And the Wise Barista will help us understand.
Somewhere in this room there is a Wise Barista who will one day...
But it's a great story anyway, isn't it?
Can we learn to listen to each other and listen to the darkness?
When we get hung up on our pride, can we be ready to apologize, you know, whoops, sorry, and trust that all we have to do is just be ourselves, just step by step, day by day, moment by moment?
And that's what today seems to be about.
Did you used to listen to Car Talk on NPR?
I feel like I should reference Click and Clack after these talks: you've wasted a perfectly good hour on Dharma talk.
Thanks.
Thanks for being here.
It's really great.

verbatim.text: Welcome, everybody. Well, we're co-creating a pretty interesting day, aren't we? Interesting, wonderful, challenging, surprising, annoying, energizing, exhausting. Just another day, really, you know, right? Just like any other day. Except we're doing it in what seems like a particular way. And I was thinking today about what seems extra interesting to me today about our sesshin practice, is the way the whole thing is like one big ritual. I think at first it might appear like it's a meditation retreat with some ritual sort of glue, so that we can manage to sit that much.

I don't think it really is that way. I think actually the whole thing is one giant ritual, one big complex ritual every moment of everything we do. You know, that the way we move and sit and stand and walk is all ritual, ritualized. The talking we do is ritual, too. Even as we try to keep the silence when we open our mouths, it's chanting. It's the usual announcements. Even this, like this is the same stuff I say every time. It's all a ritual. The eating is so ritualized.

Thank you everybody for pulling off the eating and the cooking that made the eating and the serving. So we can see that eating is a ritual. So everything is a ritual. And in fact even the zazen, which seems like some kind of meditation at first, like something we'll do in order to calm down or see things more clearly or something, the zazen is a ritual, too. Tomorrow, if you can come tomorrow morning, Chris is going to give a talk on Dogen's great essay on zazen, Fukanzazengi. And we've all chanted that many times.

So probably you noticed he says in there, zazen is not meditation, it says right in there. The word meditation, like a lot of words, gives us the idea that something's going to result or something's going to happen. Maybe it will, maybe it won't. Of course he's turning that around, helping us to see that we do things just to do them, not to get something, which is what ritual is, right? You do it just to do it. So sitting zazen, just to sit zazen.

And so I think the word in there looks like an ordinary little connector word in English, just, sit, just to sit, do zazen, just to do zazen, walk, just walk, wash the dishes, just wash the dishes, you know. It's funny, we do expect probably the dishes to be clean again, but they're going to be dirty, right? So why do we think that there's some kind of human potential, meditation something, that will clean us up so we won't get dirty again? Doesn't make sense.

So we sit just to sit as messy human beings, dirty and clean, clean and dirty. So it seems like we're doing a ritual today is all we're really doing, that we're not doing a meditation intensive exactly, but like maybe we're doing a just intensive. Re-learning how to just do things, you know. Just do one thing after the next, which isn't that complicated, but somehow we lose track of that basic ability to just do one thing.
